# An exact quadratic inequality for concave sequences

Let w_0,...,w_(N-1) be a nonnegative, nonzero concave sequence, N>=1.
Write m=max_i w_i, M=sum_i w_i, Q=sum_i w_i^2, and choose an index j
with w_j=m. Then

    Q-(2/3)m M
      >=(m^2/6)[1/(2j+1)+1/(2(N-1-j)+1)]>0.       (1)

This is an exact minimum of the quadratic expression with the indicated
peak value and index. It implies Q>(2/3)mM. It is a bounded sequence
lemma, not a statement of mixed-integer OC.

## 1. One anchored side

For an integer h>=0, consider any concave real sequence x_0,...,x_h
with x_0=1. It need not be nonnegative for this first lemma. Define

    F(x)=sum_(i=0)^h [x_i^2-(2/3)x_i].

The unique minimizer is the affine sequence

    v_i=1-2i/(2h+1),

and its value is

    F(v)=(h+1)/[3(2h+1)].                          (2)

For h=0 this is direct. Suppose h>=1 and put e_i=x_i-v_i, so e_0=0
and e is concave. For 1<=t<=h-1 define the nonnegative discrete tents

    G_t(i)=min(i,t)-it/h,    0<=i<=h.

Their second differences are minus one at t and zero elsewhere, and
both endpoints vanish. Consequently

    e_i=(i/h)e_h+sum_(t=1)^(h-1) a_t G_t(i),
    a_t=2e_t-e_(t-1)-e_(t+1)>=0.                  (3)

Indeed the difference of the two sides has zero second difference and
zero endpoints, hence is identically zero.

Set r_i=v_i-1/3=2/3-2i/(2h+1). Elementary sums of integers and squares
give

    sum_(i=0)^h r_i i=0,
    sum_(i=0)^h G_t(i)=t(h-t)/2,
    sum_(i=0)^h iG_t(i)=t(h-t)(h+t)/6.

These identities can also be obtained by splitting each sum at i=t
and summing the two affine pieces. Hence

    sum_i r_i G_t(i)
       =t(h-t)(h+1-t)/[3(2h+1)]>0.

Using (3) therefore gives sum_i r_i e_i>=0. Expanding the quadratic,

    F(x)-F(v)=sum_i e_i^2+2sum_i r_i e_i>=0.

Equality requires every e_i=0. Direct substitution of the affine v
using the same integer sums gives (2). This proves the attained
minimum and uniqueness, without a compactness or variational assumption.

## 2. Join the two sides of a peak

Divide the original sequence by m. Apply (2) to the left side of j in
reverse order, with h=j, and to the right side, with h=N-1-j. The
peak term 1-2/3=1/3 was counted twice, so subtract it once. The result is

    Q/m^2-(2/3)M/m
      >=(j+1)/[3(2j+1)]
        +(N-j)/[3(2(N-1-j)+1)]-1/3,

which simplifies to (1). Equality is realized by the two affine sides
from (2), joined at the peak. They form a nonnegative concave sequence:
the left slope is positive, the right slope is negative, and the
endpoint values are positive. For N=1 the same formula gives 1/3.

The coefficient 2/3 in the resulting homogeneous inequality cannot be
increased uniformly in N. For example take the symmetric triangular
sequence w_i=1-|i|/h on -h<=i<=h. Direct Riemann sums, or the elementary
integer formulas, give Q/(m M) tending to 2/3 as h tends to infinity.
Only this sharpness observation uses a limit; the inequality (1) is finite
and exact for every N.

## 3. A true-centroid cap consequence for interval fibers

Let actual positive interval fibers be K_i=[l_i,r_i] at consecutive
integer indices. Suppose the true unweighted mixed centroid has integer
base and continuous coordinate y. Consider any nonvertical closed
halfspace through that centroid. Translate its base by the integer mean,
then apply an affine fiber shear and, if needed, a continuous reflection,
so that the centroid is (0,0) and the halfspace is x>=0. These maps
preserve the mixed lattice, interval lengths, all cap masses, and the
centroid equations. The transformed lower sequence is convex and the
upper sequence concave. Their positive lengths w_i=r_i-l_i form a
concave sequence.

Assume this oriented cap contains no whole positive-length fiber.
Thus l_i<0 for every i. Its mass is A=sum_i (r_i)_+; it may still
exclude entire fibers with r_i<=0. The continuous mean-zero equation is

    sum_i w_i(r_i+l_i)=0.

Using r_i-l_i=w_i gives the exact identity

    sum_i w_i r_i=Q/2.

Discarding negative r_i terms and using w_i<=m yields

    m A>=sum_i w_i(r_i)_+>=Q/2.

Consequently

    A/M >= Q/(2mM)>1/3.                           (4)

This treats all finite slopes of the specified cap and includes fibers
touching its boundary at r_i=0. A fiber with l_i=0 is wholly captured
and belongs to the excluded case, as it should. The hypothesis is on
the cap's actual trace and is not omitted in (4).

The root sequence proof and this consequence do not control caps that
contain some entire fibers. In particular they do not prove the full
integer-centroid assertion or the full OC statement. They isolate a
precise remaining case with a proved strict mass bound in its complement.
